name: Tangad head comb rods

card.summary: Tangad are thin rods, with related sipit plates and saop padded boards, that were bound to infants' foreheads in the pre-colonial Visayas and Bicol to produce the broad, flat-browed head shape that was considered beautiful.
card.note: A historical practice applied to infants; head-shaping can cause asymmetry and tissue injury.

quick.overview:
Tangad is the Visayan name for a comb-like set of thin rods bound across a baby's forehead. Together with sipit (plates) and saop (padded boards), it was used in the pre-colonial central Philippines to shape the skull toward a broad face and receding forehead, which was the local ideal of beauty.

Historians describe it from Spanish-era accounts, and skulls showing the effect have been excavated at burial sites across the islands. It is a historical custom rather than a modern product, and it is documented here as part of the history of beauty standards.
quick.how: Historical accounts say the rods or boards were fastened to an infant's forehead with bandages tied at the back of the head, starting in the first weeks or months of life when the skull is soft. The pressure redirected growth so the head became wider and higher at the rear. Practitioners were families, often of high status.
quick.risks: Researchers who study artificial cranial deformation report that it can produce facial and skull asymmetry and, in the compressed areas, bleeding, infection or tissue death. It was done to infants who could not consent. It is not a current looksmaxxing practice and the devices are known mainly from historical and archaeological records.

lead: Tangad is the Visayan term for a thin rod, or comb-like set of thin rods, that was bound around an infant's forehead in the pre-colonial Philippines. Related devices were the sipit (plates or tablets) and the saop (padded boards).[1][3] They were used to flatten the forehead, and sometimes the back of the head, so that the child grew up with the broad face and sloping brow that local culture admired.[1][2]

As an appearance practice, it worked by shaping the soft infant skull so that the adult face carried the preferred proportions: a wide face, a receding forehead and a head of roughly equal length and width.[1] Flattened-forehead people were called tinangad, while unmodified people were called ondo.[1]

The practice is known from Spanish colonial writers such as the priest Diego Bobadilla in 1604 and from skulls excavated in Cebu, Samar, Bohol, Tablas and other islands.[1][3] It belongs to the wider global history of artificial cranial deformation.

chain: Rods or boards bound to an infant's forehead
Frontal bone growth is redirected backward and sideways
Broad face and receding forehead in adulthood, the local beauty ideal
angle.text: In the pre-colonial Visayas and Bicol the devices shaped the infant skull to produce a broad, flat-browed head regarded as beautiful and sometimes as a status marker. It is applied only in infancy, so it is a historical custom rather than something an adult can use.

paras: The tangad was described by historian William Henry Scott as a thin rod bound around the infant's forehead and held in place with bandages wrapped around the head.[2] Other forms used plates (sipit) or padded boards (saop), and a Spanish priest in 1604 recorded children's heads being pressed between two boards.[1]
The binding was fastened at the back of the head. It hindered forward growth of the frontal bone and directed growth backward, so the head grew higher at the rear.[1]

Early Filipinos in these groups regarded a broad face and a flattened or receding forehead as marks of beauty, with the ideal skull being about as wide as it was long.[1][2] The Spanish record says the shaping was considered a mark of beauty.[1] Nobles (tumao) may have used it as a status marker, although it is unclear whether it was restricted to them.[1]

Skulls showing the effects of binding have been recovered from burial sites in Romblon, Marinduque, Masbate, Cebu, Albay, Samar, Bohol, Surigao, Butuan and Davao.[2] Wikipedia notes Samar and Tablas as places where modified remains are found.[1]

General reviews of cranial deformation report that it can cause marked asymmetry of the face and skull, as well as bleeding, infection and tissue death in compressed areas, and that effects soften after infancy as the body compensates with growth.[1]
No studies found. Bioarchaeological work on skulls from the Philippines and on cranial modification elsewhere exists, but no clinical trials have been conducted.

timeline.event: Spanish priest Diego Bobadilla records infants' heads pressed between boards as a mark of beauty.[1]
